data.title: Real Chemistry champions health dignity initiative
data.description:
It’s human nature to want to feel seen, heard and understood. But in the context of healthcare interactions, the stakes are high, meaning moments of disconnect can threaten patients’ trust and the success of their care journey. 

Real Chemistry brings the topic to light with its “Health Dignity Initiative.”  The agency defines the term health dignity as “the experience of being seen, heard, and taken seriously” within a healthcare interaction, something that can manifest as “attentive listening, respectful treatment, clear communication and fairness in care delivery.”

"Research consistently shows that people disengage not because they’re unwilling, but because messages and interactions feel rushed, unclear, or disconnected from their lived reality," Real Chemistry's EVP, executive director of inclusive health Jewel Jones Truxon explained in a blog post about the initiative earlier this year. "Designing communications for health dignity means designing for clarity, safety, relevance, and respect across every touchpoint – ultimately leading to stronger trust, comprehension, adherence, and engagement."

According to Real Chemistry’s health dignity research, which analyzed over 200 million digital sources and surveyed 86 healthcare practitioners plus 232 patients and caregivers, 71% of people report a “dignity-defining” moment in healthcare. Online, there have been over 251,000 mentions of health dignity, with a 132% year-over-year increase in health dignity conversations. 

To address this, the health dignity initiative establishes a framework for understanding health dignity and infusing it into practice for healthcare marketers and communications, offering some key signals that play into health dignity. 

The “golden rule,” as Real Chemistry says, is treating people the way they want to be treated, as opposed to the standard code of treating others how you’d want to be treated. 

“We saw very clearly in the data how important it was for providers and for patients and caregivers to be met where they are,” Jones Truxon said in an interview. 

According to 53% of patients surveyed, “taking concerns seriously” is the most important dignity factor, while 39% say that dignity includes listening without rushing. Being rushed, ignored or spoken to using confusing jargon can compound into defining experiences, Real Chemistry explains. 

The same can be true in the opposite sense; everyday kindness can accumulate into meaningful takeaways as well. Other important signals are provider constraints and feeling safe as a patient. 

Real Chemistry lays out this concept visually in a short video that goes along with the initiative, depicting an everyday doctors’ office visit that doesn’t work out as either the patient or doctor had hoped. 

The scene takes place at the end of a woman’s visit with her physician. As the two communicate, on-screen text reveals what each is actually thinking. 

“Can you repeat that?” the patient says. “I’m exhausted,” is what she wants to say. 

The doctor glances at the clock. “We’re slammed today,” she thinks. “I have other patients waiting.”  

Still, the doctor keeps up pleasantries and continues to guide the patient through her blood test results. As the patient attempts to vocalize symptoms she’s experiencing, the doctor runs through a list of common causes, thinking it best not to speculate and worry the patient. 

Related

Patients less confident than ever about health choices: survey

“I should reassure her. I don’t want her to worry,” the doctor thinks. Meanwhile, the patient knows what she’s experiencing isn’t normal. “Please care,” she thinks. 

The doctor wants to help, a thought visually depicted by on-screen text that fills the background; “I want to help you.” 

For the patient, all she can think as the doctor talks is “she wants to leave.”

Both the patient and the doctor are visibly distressed after the visit wraps up. 

“I wish this conversation had gone differently,” they both think. 

Importantly, Real Chemistry emphasizes that these types of negative encounters have real impacts in patient engagement levels. Low levels of health dignity are “strongly associated” with delayed care seeking and negative mental health impacts. Health dignity also serves as a reputational indicator, with potential impacts across credibility and confidence for healthcare organizations that could shape key perspectives. 

“Health dignity, the experience of being seen, heard, and taken seriously, shouldn't be solely viewed as like a patient experience issue,” Jones Truxon explained. “We believe that it is a lens and could potentially show that it has implications for treatment initiation, clinical trial participation, reputation, and trust, and really understanding how people experience healthcare can help us to identify opportunities much earlier.”

Real Chemistry is “just at the beginning” of the initiative and plans to continue digging into health dignity research. Putting a name to the concept of health dignity, something that has been a “low hum conversation” for years is an important step on its own, Jones Truxon pointed out. 

Related

Real Chemistry launches AI-powered MaestroHCP to conduct omnichannel campaigns

For healthcare marketers, the concept of health dignity is crucial in ensuring messages “actually click” for the right audience, Jones Truxon said. When information gets through to the target audience, often it’s because it is delivered in a way that “truly demonstrates that we understand the audiences that we're trying to reach and engage, and they feel respected,” she said.  “They feel their dignity feels honored.”

"Real Chemistry predicts that health dignity is poised to become a defining cornerstone of the patient-HCP experience – and the patient journey," Jones Truxon explained in the blog post, noting that leaders who embrace the shift will be "better equipped to strengthen outcomes."

data.title: GSK's twin FDA wins, Roche's $15B deal and point-of-care ads
data.description:
In this week's episode of "The Top Line," we're covering a pair of FDA approvals for GSK, an antibody-drug conjugate pact worth up to $15 billion and the growing role of point-of-care advertising in pharmaceutical marketing.

First, we look at GSK's big week, which included FDA approval for Jemperli in certain patients with rectal cancer, offering the possibility of avoiding chemotherapy, radiation and surgery. The company also secured a landmark approval for Hibsago, a chronic hepatitis B treatment that could deliver a functional cure for some patients. We also discuss Roche's expanded partnership with China's Hansoh Pharmaceutical, an antibody-drug conjugate deal featuring up to $15 billion in potential milestone payments.

Then, Fierce Pharma's Zoey Becker sits down with Nicole Divinagracia, president of the Point of Care Marketing Association, to discuss the rapid growth of point-of-care advertising. Divinagracia explains what's driving that momentum, how the channel is evolving and why marketers should incorporate point of care earlier in their planning. They also explore efforts to establish more consistent measurement standards and best practices for reaching patients and healthcare professionals at critical moments in the care journey.

To learn more about the topics in this episode: 

  • GSK’s Jemperli scores FDA approval in rectal cancer, backed by high complete response rate
  • GSK brings promise of 'functional cure' to hepatitis B finish line with FDA nod for Hibsago
  • Roche returns to China’s ADC powerhouse Hansoh for $15B biobucks pact
  • Point-of-care pharma marketing spending passes $1B milestone

data.title: Vabysmo shows signs of recovery as Roche gears up for busy 2027
data.description:
After disappointing Wall Street for most of 2026, Roche’s eye disease drug Vabysmo met analysts’ expectations for the first time this year. But the company may have bigger fish to fry heading into 2027.

The bispecific antibody of VEGF-A and Ang-2 brought in 1.14 billion Swiss francs ($1.38 billion) in third-quarter sales, up 10% sequentially and topping consensus estimates by 2%.

The beat comes as Vabysmo hit a milestone, having treated 1.5 million patients globally, Roche’s pharmaceuticals chief Teresa Graham told investors during a call Thursday.

Vabysmo is a key driver in the 9% year-over-year sales growth at constant exchange rates for Roche’s ophthalmology franchise, as the drug continues market share gains, Graham said. Vabysmo is approved in the U.S. for wet age-related macular degeneration, diabetic macular edema and retinal vein occlusion. 

“By now, Vabysmo has established itself as the preferred first-line treatment, including in the U.S.,” she said.

After stellar growth initially, Vabysmo suddenly lost momentum toward the end of 2025. Between the second-quarter 2025 and the second-quarter 2026, sales of the drug actually declined 1%. 

Roche previously attributed the deceleration to a reset of the U.S. branded VEGF market after the closure of certain charity copay programs. 

“I think the U.S. has re-baselined,” Graham said on Thursday’s call. “We are expecting to remain in that low single-digit growth for Vabysmo in terms of sales."

“It’s probably important to note though that volume growth in the U.S. is much higher—there’s a contracting effect that takes effect here,” she continued. “And then, when you look ex-U.S., there is actually significant growth for Vabysmo, and more opportunity for growth and penetration to come outside of the U.S.”

The Roche exec maintained that the current consensus peak sales outlook of 6 billion Swiss francs is “very reasonable,” and that Vabysmo is on track to achieve that.

As the Vabysmo market stabilizes, Roche and investors are turning their attention to several potential blockbuster launches. 

The company’s oral SERD drug giredestrant is gearing up for an FDA decision by the end of November. For 2027, Roche is expecting FDA approvals for its KRAS G12C inhibitor divarasib in non-small cell lung cancer, for BTK inhibitor fenebrutinib in multiple sclerosis and sefaxersen in IgA nephropathy, among others. As Graham put it, Roche’s regulatory and launch teams will be “exceptionally busy” in the next few months. 

None of those will be easy rollouts. For giredestrant, the company is targeting a first-in-class adjuvant nod for early breast cancer, but as one analyst noted on the call, many doctors remain skeptical and are waiting for overall survival data to be convinced. The phase 3 lidERA trial supporting Roche’s filing will have another overall survival data cutoff toward the first half of 2027, Graham noted. 

As for another criticism around lidERA’s lack of involvement of a CDK4/6 inhibitor, Graham said that a single-arm sub-study in combination with Eli Lilly’s Verzenio is expected to read out this year. Roche recently also announced two new studies in the adjuvant setting, including an investigator-initiated study using a ctDNA-guided approach and a phase 1/3 testing giredestrant alongside Pfizer’s CDK4 candidate atirmociclib.

Related

Despite data concerns, Roche’s oral SERD can still be largest product in company history: exec

For divarasib, Roche will need to compete with existing KRAS inhibitors, Amgen’s Lumakras and Bristol Myers Squibb’s Krazati. After seeing “strong” phase 3 data, to be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology 2026 Congress this weekend, Roche has increased divarasib’s peak sales guidance to between 2 billion and 3 billion Swiss francs, Roche’s CEO Thomas Schinecker said on the call.

In the BTK field, Roche’s fenebrutinib is on a collision course with Novartis’ Rhapsido in MS. It’s also not entirely clear how the oral BTK space will play out against antibody drugs such as Roche’s top-selling Ocrevus, although Graham argued fenebrutinib “will ultimately just crack up a whole new market segment,” rather than chipping away Ocrevus’ market. 

As for IgAN, the space has become crowded with multiple options across various mechanisms of action, including a new FDA nod Wednesday for AstraZeneca’s complement inhibitor Ultomiris. 

Despite the upcoming launches, one analyst on the call questioned Roche’s ability to maintain the same level of revenue growth in 2027, pointing to “growth pressures or slowdowns on a number of products.” In the first nine months of 2026, Roche’s pharmaceuticals division ginned up 36.2 billion Swiss francs ($44 billion) on the strength of a 7% year-over-year increase at constant exchange rates, and the entire group’s 46.5 billion Swiss francs marked 6% growth. 

“I can only say that we’re confident that we can maintain a similar momentum that we have,” Schinecker said on the call, adding that profit margins are expected to be “at least stable.”

data.title: AbbVie pumps up the case for early subcutaneous Parkinson’s care
data.description:
Delaying the use of subcutaneous Parkinson’s disease treatments by one year increases annual medical costs by 59.1%, AbbVie-sponsored research found.

The study, which researchers will present (PDF) at the AMCP Nexus Conference this month, modeled the impact of delaying the initiation of two subcutaneous therapies by one year. One therapy comprised foslevodopa and foscarbidopa, the combination that AbbVie sells as Vyalev. The other therapy featured apomorphine, the active ingredient in Supernus Pharmaceuticals’ Onapgo. 

In the model, patients who received oral standard of care for one year had worse outcomes than their peers who started subcutaneous therapy immediately. Over three years, delayed treatment resulted in 2.3 more OFF hours per patient per day, on average. The delayed cohort experienced 0.9 more OFF hours per day at Year 3, despite having been on the subcutaneous treatment for two years at that point.

Annual medical costs per patient were $22,233 higher in the delayed-treatment cohort. Researchers attributed the 59.1% increase in costs to additional emergency room visits, hospitalizations and nursing home care. Delayed care was associated with other knock-on costs. Reduced work productivity in the delayed cohort resulted in an annual loss of $2,614 per patient and caregiver.

The researchers framed the results as evidence that “relatively modest delays in optimal treatment initiation can have substantial downstream clinical, humanistic, economic and societal consequences.”

That conclusion echoes findings from a study shared early this month at the 2026 International Congress of Parkinson’s Disease and Movement Disorders (MDS). The studies used the same approach to model the effect of delaying the use of the same subcutaneous therapies, and both reported 2.3 additional OFF hours per day. 

The MDS study dug deeper into the clinical consequences of the OFF hours. Researchers linked delayed treatment to two extra falls, as well as increases in nursing home days and hospital nights of 97.6% and 60.2%, respectively, over three years. Hospitalizations, emergency room visits and long-term care use increased by 45.8%, 48.8% and 31.9%, respectively. 

AbbVie could benefit if the findings encourage physicians to start patients on subcutaneous therapy earlier. Sales of Vyalev, which the FDA approved two years ago, reached $457 million over the first half of the year. With sales rising 27% sequentially in the second quarter, Vyalev is “well on track to achieve blockbuster sales this year,” AbbVie Chief Commercial Officer Jeffrey Stewart said on a July earnings call. 

Sales of Onapgo, which received FDA approval in February 2025, totaled $21.9 million in the first six months of this year. Supply constraints have limited sales. Supernus aims to receive FDA approval for a second supplier by mid-2027.

data.title: Direct-to-patient pharma programs transform drug access: survey
data.description:
Many direct-to-patient (DTP) programs have significantly affected access to medicines, a survey of U.S. life sciences leaders found.

Almost three years after the launch of Eli Lilly’s LillyDirect platform, the biopharma industry has a growing body of evidence of DTP’s impact. Phil, which partners with drugmakers on the programs, shed light on that impact by surveying 74 people, 70% of whom said DTP initiatives have had a transformative or significant impact on access to medicines. 

The programs are similarly impactful for the drugmakers themselves. Almost one-third of respondents called DTP “mission critical.” A further 46% of respondents described DTP programs as very important. 

DTP programs supporting multiple brands are in place at 42% of the surveyed organizations, with a further 16% of respondents operating platforms for a single brand. About 20% of respondents aim to launch a DTP program in the next year. The remaining 23% are exploring DTP but are yet to commit to establishing a platform. 

Companies with established programs continue to refine and improve their offerings. More than half of manufacturers are actively using AI, and a further 36% are piloting or exploring the technology. Most respondents have had positive experiences with AI. Only 15% said the technology fell short of their expectations. AI met or exceeded 62% and 23% of users’ expectations, respectively. 

Phil identified specialty support as another fast-growing area of DTP expansion. Branded retail and other medications with moderate access needs were early additions to DTP programs, but specialty support is rising. Support is in place at 65% of established DTP programs. That figure is forecast to rise to 90% within 12 months. Support is rarer at emerging programs, 15% of which have specialty capabilities today. 

Many respondents are measuring the impact of their programs, most frequently by their effect on patient satisfaction, refill adherence and patient starts. Respondents aim to provide multiple affordability pathways, flexible intake options and speed of access.

data.title: FDA finalizes guidance on prescription drug apps
data.description:
The FDA is codifying its regulations around mobile apps that go along with prescription drugs, offering a clearer framework for drug companies that want to get in on the evolving digital health technology landscape. 

Through a final guidance (PDF) on the topic released Oct. 20, the agency is ending “longstanding uncertainty” with recommendations on which in-app content is subject to FDA submission requirements, when apps should be included in drug labeling and more, it explained in a press release.

Importantly, the guidance groups two distinct categories of mobile apps or “companion software,” with each subject to different regulations. Apps connected to a medical device, such as those that go along with an asthma inhaler, for example, should be included in the associated drug’s official prescription label, as the technology plays a key role in how the product is used. 

Meanwhile, “standalone apps” like symptom trackers, dose reminders or health coaching tools should only show up on a drug’s prescribing label if the drugmaker is able to demonstrate that the app is necessary for safe and effective use or can prove a meaningful clinical benefit, the FDA said. If not, that information will be treated as promotional labeling, not FDA-required labeling. 

In most cases, the agency said, content that a standalone companion app shows its users will be treated as promotional material, and “consistent with how the FDA handles other drug advertising.”

As the FDA’s deputy commissioner for technology Jared Seehafer pointed out, companion apps are “quickly moving beyond simple dose reminders toward tools that adapt to each patient,” he said in the agency release. “Finalizing this guidance gives drug companies and their technology partners a stable foundation to build on as these technologies advance and helps ensure patients and providers can trust the information they receive.”

Related

Merck KGaA, Huma collab bears fruit with launch of bladder cancer patient support app

“This guidance reflects FDA’s commitment to responsible, risk-proportionate oversight of digital health, an area that is a key priority for the agency and is evolving rapidly and holds significant promise for improving patient care,” director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evolution and Research (CDER) Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D. added. “By aligning our approach across drug and device centers, we are giving developers a clear and consistent pathway to bring safe, effective digital health technologies to patients.”

When the draft guidance that the new final guidance replaces originally came out in 2023, legal experts at global law firm Sheppard called the move a “significant step” in the formation of the FDA’s regulatory framework for digital health products, an area that is “consistently evolving to keep up with the rapid pace of innovation.”

Mobile apps were once a major innovative addition to certain drug devices that have now become the norm in products like continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) for diabetes. On the pharma side, meanwhile, in-app counterparts are used as another key marketing tool reflective of the recent migration away from linear TV as the primary outreach channel for pharma advertising. 

In 2020, WEGO Health found that while in-house pharma apps weren’t taking off as much with patients, companies were finding success in collaborations with other app makers. The sentiment rings true today, with several tie-ins popping up to help companies boost awareness within their treatment areas. 

Eisai, for one, recently teamed up with the Pokémon Sleep app to raise awareness of the importance of good sleep, while Daré Bioscience laid the groundwork for its female sexual arousal drug launch by partnering with women’s health app Rosy Wellness on a series of sexual health education content promoting and explaining the product. 

This summer, Bausch + Lomb rolled out a dry eye disease education push through Verily Me, offering expanded information about dry eye disease risk factors, symptoms and treatment options through the app. AI platforms such as Verily Me have carved out a niche of their own in the digital space recently, building on the popularity of AI tools and providing patients with a free and accessible route to personalized health advice. 

With the rapid evolution of AI tech and other digital software, the FDA emphasized its “ongoing commitment to modernizing its regulatory framework” to keep pace, it said in its Oct. 20 release, pledging to “reduce unnecessary uncertainty for developers and manufacturers” while keeping the safety and effectiveness standards many rely on.

data.title: AbbVie hits the gas on immunology awareness with McLaren F1 pact
data.description:
AbbVie has formed a multiyear deal with the McLaren Formula 1 team, signing up to raise awareness of immune-mediated diseases and provide funding for global charities.

Illinois-based AbbVie will launch its “Race to Innovate” campaign with McLaren at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, Texas, this weekend. The global attention on the U.S. Grand Prix makes the race weekend “a powerful moment” to introduce the partnership, AbbVie said. As an official pharmaceutical partner of the McLaren Formula 1 team, AbbVie will expand the campaign throughout the 2027 season. 

Through the campaign, AbbVie will donate $10,000 to global charities for every 10 points that McLaren earns in the Constructors’ Championship. Last season, McLaren won the Constructors’ Championship with 833 points. This season, McLaren is third going into the U.S. Grand Prix with 339 points. 

The partnership echoes the alliance that AbbVie struck recently with the PGA Tour and the 2026 Presidents Cup. Through that partnership, AbbVie will donate to patient advocacy organizations for every birdie at PGA Tour Signature Events and the FedEx Cup Playoffs. AbbVie formed the golf deal to raise awareness and advance support for people living with neurological and mental health conditions.

Between the McLaren and PGA deals, AbbVie has secured sponsorships for the two cornerstones of its business—immunology and neuroscience—in quick succession. Immunology, the area covered by the McLaren deal, accounted for more than half of AbbVie’s revenues in the second quarter as the company continued to grow Skyrizi and Rinvoq to mitigate the erosion of Humira sales. 

The Formula 1 partnership is the latest in a series of alliances between McLaren and pharmaceutical companies. GSK formed a five-year pact with McLaren in 2011, tapping the automotive manufacturer for expertise in engineering, technology, analytics and strategy modeling. In 2022, Sanofi partnered with McLaren Racing on manufacturing efficiency and performance. 

Multiple drugmakers have struck sponsorship agreements with U.S. motorsport teams. Eli Lilly, Novo and Pfizer are among the companies to sponsor IndyCar and NASCAR teams. Vanda Pharmaceuticals joined IndyCar’s list of pharma sponsors in July, when it backed the No. 47 car to raise awareness of its motion sickness pill Nereus.

data.title: Viola Davis opens up about shingles experience in GSK campaign
data.description:
Legendary actress Viola Davis’s newest role sees her getting real about shingles as a GSK spokesperson, reminding others that anyone, even world-famous stars, have a risk of getting “shingles, actually" as they age. 

In GSK’s educational “Shingles, actually” campaign, the “How to Get Away with Murder” star opens up about her personal experience with shingles for the first time, getting candid about the shingles-related realities of aging and encouraging other adults over 50 years old to discuss preventative options with their healthcare providers. 

In a video for the campaign, Davis starts off with an earnest appeal to “everyone over 50,” encouraging the audience to reflect on “everything that’s brought you to this moment,” she says. 

“Sure, you’ve heard of shingles and may think it won’t happen to you. I didn’t think so either. But don’t be like me,” she insists, explaining that 99% of adults aged 50 years and older already carry the virus that causes shingles.

Davis is a unique case in that she contracted shingles more than once. For her, the pain she experienced from shingles was a “9 out of 10.”

“I couldn’t go out, I couldn’t work,” she said. 

In the video, Davis walks into a doctor’s office, where social media personality and family medicine physician Jen Caudle is explaining similar stats to a patient. Together, the two discuss how the immune system naturally weakens with age. 

Later in the video, Davis meets with another shingles patient advocate, Phil, who shares his own experience with the painful rash before she continues her one-on-one chat with the camera about how “as you age, you have to be your own health advocate,” she explained, emphasizing that her message is “no script, no filters, just real talk.”

In another video, Davis and Caudle chat in a podcast setting in front of microphones, discussing similar themes and getting into the health risk of shingles in a candid tone. For Davis, shingles was “not on my radar,” and she was “completely caught off guard” by the rash and other effects, she said. 

“We just need to be real with each other about what aging actually looks like. Our lives haven’t slowed down; we feel great, and we’re leaning in,” Davis commented in a GSK release. “But it’s still true that our age puts us at increased risk for certain things, like shingles. If one in three people develop shingles in their lifetime, why do we always think we won’t be the one?”

“Shingles, actually” and "myth-busting" 

“Shingles, actually” is the second coming of “THRIVE@50+,” a previous GSK shingles campaign targeted at the 50 years old and up demographic that touted supermodel Brooke Shields as its primary spokesperson. The awareness push centered on aging and how shingles vaccination is one way people over 50 can “protect their power,” as Shields said in a three-minute film that went along with the campaign. 

Related

GSK makes Brooke Shields the star of shingles vaccination push

But, as GSK later found out, people wanted “real stories” about shingles and the realities of aging- “the good, the bad, the everything in between,” the company’s director of U.S. vaccines communications Abby Capobianco explained in an interview. 

“Shingles, actually” accomplishes that goal with perhaps one of the most recognizable and respected voices out there in Davis. While she might not be inherently relatable, as most people don’t have the prestigious EGOT status by winning an Emmy Award, Grammy Award, Oscar and Tony Award, Davis far and beyond “carries that gravity and that trust,” Capobianco said. 

Aside from being a recognized face and voice, Davis sharing her story of contracting shingles goes to show that anyone can get shingles, even a world-famous actress. 

In vaccine marketing, hearing immunization or preventative options encouraged by a trusted source is particularly important for increasing vaccination rates. As senior director of consumer experience and marketing Robert Johnstone puts it, hearing these experiences firsthand is what “drives action” and makes people “take their health seriously.” 

GSK is pushing its “Shingles, actually” messaging through a dedicated Instagram channel that will provide regular videos on disease education through influential voices and shingles advocates. With over 6,000 followers so far, the page is so far hopping on viral trends such as the “pass the phone” challenge, featuring appearances from other GSK celebrity spokespeople like “Sex and the City” star Kristin Davis. 

“Shingles, actually was inspired by all of you,” one Instagram caption reads. “We are creating the space for real and candid conversations about aging and the health risks we face, like shingles.”

Instagram and newer social media channels aren't typically considered a prime way to reach the over 50 year-old audience, but as it turns out, another reality of modern aging is that older adults are actually “very tuned in” to the platform, Capobianco said. To her point, Davis’ campaign video has racked up nearly 30,000 likes on GSK’s campaign Instagram page, with hundreds of comments chiming in to support, share personal shingles stories and even express newfound interest in getting vaccinated. 

Additionally, GSK will run the hero video on YouTube, a “big, big platform” for its target audience, Capobianco noted. According to Pew Research Center, 85% of adults surveyed aged 50 to 64 in 2025 reported using YouTube, while 40% are on Instagram. 

GSK’s campaign is “myth-busting” in a lot of ways, Johnstone noted, dispelling both the narrative that adults over 50 aren’t social media-savvy but also that they are “too young, too healthy” to get shingles. 

“Most people are aware of shingles, but they underestimate the impact of shingles,” Johnstone explained. “Just helping to bring that to life for consumers, I think, is really important.” 

At age 50, many are “taking control of their health narrative,” Capobianco said. “It’s important that health risks like shingles be included in that health narrative.”

GSK’s shingles vaccine Shingrix, which isn’t mentioned by name across “Shingles, actually,” is a strong driver of the company’s vaccine sales, amassing £1.9 billion ($2.5 million) in yearly sales as of this year’s second quarter, GSK reported in July. 

Back in April, new CEO Luke Miels explained that the drugmaker is focusing on the subpopulation within the 70 million unvaccinated people above 50 who are “more motivated” with an “intent to get vaccinated,” he said on a quarterly earnings call.

data.title: The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Lilly, Novo underwent minor fluctuations
data.description:
With the recent launches of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo, the obesity market has started to shift toward oral GLP-1 drugs. While Novo leverages its first-mover advantage with the familiar Wegovy brand, Lilly is betting that the freedom from strict fasting and water requirements can give Foundayo an edge.

Each week, Fierce Pharma’s Oral GLP-1 Tracker will leverage analysts’ notes and IQVIA data to monitor prescription trends and shifting market shares as these two titans vie to become the go-to oral weight-loss solution for millions.

UPDATED: Oct. 16, 2026

The previous week was rather uneventful for the two oral GLP-1 drugs as Americans geared up for another national holiday, Columbus Day.

Total prescriptions for Novo's Wegovy pill dipped about 3% sequentially to approximately 173.5K last week. Again, the script number was the result of a compromise between Citi's reported 173K and Jefferies' 174K, both referencing IQVIA.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo scripts ticked up about 4% to 60,151, still shy of the small molecule's previous record of 64,268.

In the broader obesity market, Lilly's Zepbound remained the leader with about 801.8K total scripts, relatively flat week over week. All Wegovy scripts across its injectable and oral forms trended 2.5% downward and landed at about 492.6K, according to Citi.

Earlier this week, drug regulators at the European Medicines Agency recommended a marketing authorization in the European Union for Foundayo for both weight management and Type 2 diabetes in adults. The European Commission is expected to sign off on the approval in a few weeks. 

UPDATED: Oct. 9, 2026

Prescriptions for Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill pulled back a little during the last week. 

In its 26th week of launch, Foundayo achieved 57,920 total scripts, down 9.9% sequentially, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

For oral Wegovy, Citi said IQVIA recorded roughly 179K scripts, while Jefferies quoted 180K. To reconcile the discrepancy between the two numbers, we used 179.5K, which translates into a 1.4% weekly decline.

In fact, scripts for all major GLP-1s declined last week across diabetes and obesity care, save for Lilly's Zepbound KwikPen, a prefilled injection pen that delivers four fixed weekly doses of tirzepatide, according to Jefferies. Overall Zepbound scripts dipped below 800K in a 0.8% decrease sequentially, just as Novo's total Wegovy scripts fell 2.7% to 505.5K, according to Citi.

Based on the numbers, Jefferies now models $208 million for Foundayo sales in the third quarter, which the team noted is in line with consensus.

UPDATED: Oct. 2, 2026

Eli Lilly's Foundayo is showing clearer signs of acceleration. Total prescriptions for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist surged about 21% to 64,268 during last week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. That haul came off a 13% sequential increase the week before that.

"We're seeing early signs of growth in Q3 for Foundayo," Jefferies analysts wrote in an Oct. 2 note.

Recent expansion of Foundayo could be attributed to a direct-to-consumer ad first aired in late August featuring Martha Stewart, as well as the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program which, as of July, offers eligible seniors GLP-1 obesity drugs at a $50 monthly copay.

Meanwhile, Novo's Wegovy pill scripts appear stuck at just above $180K. Except for a Labor Day holiday lull, total weekly scripts for the oral semaglutide product have hovered between 181K and 184K over the past five weeks, including 182K last week, according to Citi.

It's worth noting that Foundayo took 25 weeks to reach what the Wegovy pill achieved in just seven weeks in terms of total scripts. But the gap between the two drugs is closing. As Jefferies noted, Lilly owned 26% of the oral obesity market as of last week, versus a little less than 23% in the previous two weeks.

Foundayo’s launch so far does compare favorably to that of Novo’s injected Wegovy, which numbered 1,578 prescriptions through two weeks when it reached the market in the U.S. but falls short of Lilly’s Zepbound pen, which counted 7,292 prescriptions through its second week.

In its note to investors, analysts from Jefferies called the result “disappointing vs. expectations."

Brand recognition has played a role, according to Bernstein analyst Courtney Breen, who said that online searches for GLP-1 drugs peaked during Wegovy’s launch, potentially boosting demand.

UPDATE: April 21, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo is off to a solid launch, drawing 1,390 prescriptions in its first week on the market, according to tracking figures from IQVIA and presented by Jefferies. The tabulation is from the week starting April 6. This compares to the 3,071 prescriptions Novo Nordisk garnered during its Wegovy pill launch week in January.

While Foundayo came up short in this oral GLP-1 launch week comparison, it did exceed the number of prescriptions recorded in the first week of the launch of both Lilly’s injected Zepbound (1,100) and Novo’s injected version of Wegovy (768).

In a note to clients, analysts with Jefferies cautioned that comparisons can be “tricky” given that oral Wegovy was launched at the start of the year and that initial capture rates from IQVIA are “volatile” and may not include product sampling. 

“Overall, we think Foundayo’s initial scripts look excellent,” the Jefferies team wrote, adding that it is modeling Foundayo’s sales to reach $1.6 billion this year, compared to a consensus of $1.5 billion, with its peak annual sales topping out at $30 billion versus the consensus of $26 billion. 

“We think the real opportunity for Foundayo is ex-U.S., given its clear advantages on scale, distribution and [cost of goods sold],” Jefferies wrote.

data.title: Sanofi joins the peloton as '27 Tour de France partner
data.description:
Sanofi is gearing up for another major sports sponsorship in its home country, this time with the 2027 Tour de France.

The French pharma will be the first company to sponsor the prestigious white jersey, which recognizes the best rider under 25, at both the Tour de France and the women's Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift.

Sanofi will use the sponsorship and the races' massive global reach to “engage the public on health and science education” through initiatives developed in collaboration with patient organizations and healthcare professionals, it said in an Oct. 16 release. The programs will focus on prevention and patient support and take place throughout 2027 in stage towns, fan zones, along the race routes and online.

Between 10 million and 12 million spectators line the Tour de France route each year, providing a major audience alongside the estimated 150 million TV viewers the race reaches in Europe and broadcasts in 190 countries, according to Sanofi.

“The Tour de France has a unique ability to reach millions of people across France and around the world. We are harnessing this extraordinary reach in service of health,” Sanofi CEO Belén Garijo commented in the release. “Just like a cycling team in the peloton, where riders succeed by working together, we believe scientific progress is also a collective effort. Through the power of sport, we can connect with people, raise awareness of diseases and prevention, and make health information more accessible.”

In a one-minute video accompanying the announcement of Sanofi as a major partner of the race, the drugmaker further connects the cycling competition to “the race for better health," with a montage of fast-paced cyclists and cheering spectators interspersed with footage from Sanofi's labs.

“We’ll ride alongside the next generation of men and women who will compete for the white jersey and the future it represents,” a voiceover says, as the video shows a cyclist wearing the Sanofi-branded white jersey, complete with sleeve stripes and shorts in Sanofi's signature purple. “Like us, they know what it takes to keep going until they cross the finish line.”

The video calls the 2027 launch Sanofi's “largest health awareness campaign” and ends with a visualization of the race route outlined in Sanofi purple.

“Wherever the tour goes, we go,” the voiceover says. “The race for health is on.”

The partnership reflects both Sanofi's recent history of sponsoring major sporting events and its shared French roots with the Tour de France, bringing together “two institutions born in France and now recognized around the world,” Sanofi explained, noting that the two “share a commitment to excellence and endurance.”

By sponsoring both the women's and men's races, the company reflects a “coherent and inclusive vision of sport, excellence and visibility,” it added in an FAQ.

Through its recent sports partnerships, Sanofi has carved out a niche in “turning global reach into meaningful health impact,” as the company put it in the release.

In 2024, Sanofi launched what it called at the time the “biggest corporate activation” in its history during the Summer Olympics in Paris. The marketing push included digital activations throughout the event and its “Igniting Potential” campaign, which drew parallels between Sanofi scientists and Olympic athletes.

Last year, the company used the 24 Hours of Le Mans auto race to raise meningitis awareness by displaying the meningitis flag on two-time Le Mans winner United Autosports' No. 59 McLaren during the race, with the team's drivers also sporting the flag's colors.

More recently, Sanofi returned to the Olympic stage as an official health partner of the Special Olympics Unified Football World Cup in Paris. Also this year, the company sponsored Boston's involvement in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with its head of external engagement, Tanisha Sullivan, joining an advisory board supporting the city's preparations for the tournament.

Elsewhere, Sanofi is using pickleball to encourage older adults to protect themselves against COVID-19 with its Nuvaxovid vaccine through a “Serve Up Protection” campaign with USA Pickleball. The company expanded its sports-related partnerships for Nuvaxovid with a new celebrity spokesperson, NBA champion Karl-Anthony Towns, who helped lead the New York Knicks to their first NBA title in 53 years this year.
